pages.name: Area times speed
pages.task: Air crosses a 0.5 m² opening at 2 m/s. What flow of air passes through it?
pages.why: In one second the air moves 2 m. So a block of air 0.5 m² across and 2 m long passes through. Its volume is 0.5 × 2 = 1 m³. So 1 m³ passes each second.

pages.name: Spare current makes gas
pages.text: This full battery of 24 cells, 100 Ah each, is still on charge. Near full, the plates take less of the current. The rest splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. That is [[gassing]]. Past the gassing voltage, 2.40 V a cell, the limit is 2.5 to 5 A per 100 Ah. A failed charger pushing 20 A gives four to eight times that, and the bubbles run thick.

Air comes in low on the left and leaves high on the right. A hydrogen gauge from 0 to 5 per cent, with marks at 0.4 and 1, shaded from 4, where hydrogen ignites. The limit for this room, 0.4, is lit. Its level is between 0.4 and 1. Each opening face-on, to scale: the real opening is a solid square, and the opening the rule asks for is a dashed square, the same size.

pages.name: Two limits
pages.text: Hydrogen in air ignites from about 4 to 75 per cent. Figures vary slightly. A room people enter is held below 0.4 per cent, a tenth of 4. An enclosure nobody enters may reach 1 per cent, a quarter of 4. Each limit becomes a [[dilution factor]], S. A room people enter takes S = 10, since 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4. An enclosure takes S = 4, since 4 ÷ 4 = 1.

pages.name: One per cent
pages.task: A battery room's hydrogen reads 1 per cent, and people work in it. Is that within the limit?
pages.answer: No: a room people enter must stay below 0.4 per cent
pages.why: People work in this room, so S = 10. Its limit is 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4 per cent, and 1 per cent is well over it. 1 per cent is already a quarter of the way to 4 per cent, where hydrogen ignites. The 1 per cent limit is only for an enclosure nobody enters.

pages.name: The rule
pages.text: The inlet and the outlet each need at least 0.3 × N × I × S cm². N is the number of cells, I the current in amps, and S the dilution factor. For 24 cells at 20 A in a room people enter, that is 0.3 × 24 × 20 × 10 = 1440 cm². The dashed outline draws it to scale. With 12 cells, it halves to 720 cm².

pages.name: An enclosure
pages.task: The same 24 cells at 20 A sit in an enclosure nobody enters. What opening does each vent need?
pages.why: An enclosure takes S = 4. So each opening needs 0.3 × 24 × 20 × 4 = 576 cm². An enclosure may hold up to 1 per cent hydrogen, more than a room people enter. So it needs less air, and a smaller opening.

pages.name: Size for the fault
pages.text: I is the most current the charger is likely to deliver if it fails. On float, this battery takes an example 0.5 A. Sized for float, each opening would need just 36 cm². But a failed charger can push its full 20 A into the full battery. Most of that current becomes gas. So the opening needed grows forty times, to 1440 cm².

pages.name: Float or fault?
pages.task: A 24-cell battery floats at 0.5 A in a room people enter. If its control failed, its charger could push 20 A. What opening do the vents need?
pages.why: Size from the fault current, not the float current. A failed charger can push 20 A into the full battery, and that spare current splits water. So each opening needs 0.3 × 24 × 20 × 10 = 1440 cm². Sized for float, 36 cm² would be forty times too small.

pages.name: Air carries it away
pages.text: The rule assumes air crosses each opening at 0.1 m/s or more. Flow = area × speed, so 1440 cm² passes 14.4 litres a second. At 10 A, the hydrogen reads 0.2 per cent. Halve the opening: the same gas meets half the air, so the hydrogen doubles, to 0.4 per cent. If the room relies on a fan and it fails, the hydrogen climbs past 1 per cent.

pages.name: Blocked opening
pages.task: Stores now block half of the 1440 cm² opening, leaving 720 cm². The charger fails and pushes 20 A into the 24 cells. What does the hydrogen reach?
pages.why: Through the full 1440 cm², 20 A holds this room at the 0.4 per cent limit. Half the opening lets in half the air, and the same gas spreads through it. So the hydrogen doubles, to 0.8 per cent. That is twice the limit for a room people enter.

pages.name: Sealed cells
pages.text: A [[valve-regulated]] cell is sealed, with a valve on top. It keeps most of its gas inside and turns it back into water. So its bubbles fade, and the hydrogen readout shows no number. A hard charge still builds pressure inside. Past an example 10 A, the pressure lifts the valve, and gas escapes. So sealed means much less gas, not none.

pages.name: Board over the vents?
pages.task: Sealed, valve-regulated cells replace a flooded battery. Someone suggests boarding over the vents. Are they right?
pages.answer: No: the cells make much less gas, but their valves can still let it out
pages.why: Sealed cells keep most of their gas and turn it back into water. But a hard charge builds pressure, and the valve lets gas out. A failed charger pushes just that kind of current. So the room still needs its vents.

pages.task: A room people enter holds 55 cells. The charger can deliver 10 A if it fails. What opening does each vent need?
pages.why: People enter, so S = 10. Each opening needs 0.3 × 55 × 10 × 10 = 1650 cm². That is 0.165 m². At 0.1 m/s it passes 0.0165 m³ of air a second, or 16.5 litres. The 1440 cm² openings drawn here fall short, so the hydrogen sits above the 0.4 per cent limit.

pages.name: The fan stops
pages.task: A battery room's fan stops during an equalise. What happens to the hydrogen?
pages.answer: It keeps climbing towards the 4 per cent band
pages.why: An equalise is a deliberate overcharge, so most of its current becomes gas. The sizing assumes air keeps crossing the openings. With the fan stopped, nothing carries the gas out. So the hydrogen keeps climbing towards 4 per cent, where it ignites.

pages.name: Charger off
pages.task: A hard charge has just finished, and the charger is off. Someone wants to start work by the battery that could make a spark. Can they start now?
pages.answer: No: leave the battery to stand for at least 20 minutes first
pages.why: Switching off stops new gas, but not the gas already made. It still has to clear from the cells and the room. So leave the battery to stand for at least 20 minutes after charging. Only then start work that could make a spark.
